The record's own 'held' list for west2368 does not include this file (it sits under the Eastern Balochi key), and its provenance is a shadow-library mirror per that. (2) Deciding source: a 2009 handbook chapter (grammar-sketch class) by the field's two specialists, summarising Axenov 2006 (335-pp reference grammar, pp. 48-50), Rastorgueva 1966, Moshkalo 1991, Buddruss 1988 — second-hand but authoritative; the held Korn 2003 thesis sec. II.1.3 pp. 67-70 gives the same rules in more detail (Turkmenistan: final as a rule; -án always accented; -ē, pronominal suffixes, singular case endings enclitic; na-/ma- accented; irrealis b- forms initial). sources.quote: "For the Western Balochi dialect of Turkmenistan (cf. Axenov 2006: 48-50, partly revising Rastorgueva 1966: 328f., 334-336; Moshkalo 1991: 40, 67ff.) and Afghanistan (Buddruss 1988: 45ff.), a system of stress has been noted which is similar to that of New Persian. The stress is on the last syllable of the word as a rule, except for the individuation marker (see 4.2) -e, the pronominal suffixes and the present copula, which are enclitic." (Jahani & Korn 2009: 648)

sources.quote: Intro repeats J&K: 'in Western dialects such as in Sarhaddi Balochi, the stress is on the last syllable of a word' (p. 80-81, citing Jahani & Korn 2009). But her own pooled analysis of the three Iranian dialects (two of them Western: Mirjaveh Sarhaddi, Sarawani; 12 informants, Zahedan 2010-14) is quantity-sensitive: 'the placement of stress in mono-morphemic words is largely predictable, in regularly falling on the rightmost heavy syllable' (p. 81); 'the rightmost CVV syllable attracts primary stress, but if a word has no bimoraic syllable ... then CVC syllable surfaces as heavy and receives p

sources.citation: Jahani, Carina. 2019. A Grammar of Modern Standard Balochi. Studia Iranica Upsaliensia 36. Uppsala: Acta Universitatis Upsaliensis (open access, DiVA diva2:1372275; fetched sources via Wayback).
sources.quote: 'Stress normally falls on the last syllable of the word for nouns and adjectives. Some pronouns, adverbs, adpositions, conjunctions and interjections take their stress on the first syllable. ... All clitics ... are unstressed. Stress also varies in different dialects, and divergences from the normal stress patterns are not uncommon. (It may, in fact, be more appropriate to call this feature tone than to call it stress.)' Indirect for west2368: the standard described is built on Southern Balochi dialects (p. 20), not Western; consistent with final-stress-as-norm but not evidence for the Western

I: 2, 34, 179ff.) as patterning with weight-sensitive Karachi Balochi; the sweep read only vol. 1 sec. 1.104 online and found no explicit word-stress rule. Needed to decide whether the strict-final coding holds across the languoid or only for Turkmenistan/Afghanistan.
